issues.legal_issue: A finding on title made incidentally in a small-cause rent suit does not bar a later regular civil suit that directly raises title to immovable property.
material_facts: Earlier suits sought recovery of rent and relied on a document that purported to transfer the house and create a tenancy.
The small-cause court found that the document was a sale deed and decreed the rent claims.
A later regular civil suit directly sought a declaration of ownership and alleged that the sale document was nominal.
issues.conclusion: The small-cause court’s finding that the document was a sale deed did not operate as res judicata in the later suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, res judicata requires that the matter was directly and substantially in issue in the former suit and was heard and finally decided. A matter in issue only collaterally or incidentally cannot support the bar. A title finding in a small-cause suit is incidental to its substantial issue and cannot bar a later regular suit directly raising title to immovable property. Explanation VIII to section 11 applies only when the issue was heard and finally decided in the earlier suit. The Court approved Poholi Mullick v. Fukeer Chunder Patnaik, Chet Ram v. Ganga, Anwar Ali v. Nur-Ul-Haq, Khandu Valad Keru v. Tatia Valad Vithoba, Mohd. Yusuf v. Abdul Wahid, and S.A.A. Annamalai Chettiar v. Molaiyan; it distinguished the general res judicata principles discussed in Gulabchand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Bombay.

predicates.small_cause_rent_proceeding: A court of small causes decided an earlier claim for rent in which title to the property arose.
predicates.later_regular_property_suit: A later regular civil suit directly sought determination or enforcement of a right or interest in immovable property.
predicates.title_issue_incidental: The earlier court considered title only incidentally while deciding the substantial issue in the rent claim.

issues.definition: When a small-cause rent proceeding considers title only incidentally and a later regular property suit directly raises title, the earlier title finding does not bar the later suit.

issues.legal_issue: The bar on oral evidence concerning the terms of a written transaction does not prevent a party from proving that the transaction recorded in the document was never intended to operate and that a different transaction was made.
material_facts: A document purported to record a sale and a rent arrangement.
The party resisting the document’s effect alleged that it was nominal, was never intended to be acted upon, and that the actual arrangement was a loan secured by the property.
The trial court permitted oral evidence supporting that allegation.
issues.conclusion: Section 92(1) did not bar the oral evidence; the evidence was admissible to show that the document was a sham and that a different transaction had been made.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 92(1) of the Indian Evidence Act require the terms and nature of a transaction to be derived from the document when a party relies on it, and generally bar oral evidence between the parties to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from its terms. That bar does not apply when a party asserts that the transaction recorded in the document was never intended to operate and that a different transaction altogether was made. The Court followed Tyagaraja Mudaliyar v. Vedathanni and also noted the first proviso to section 92, which permits proof of facts that invalidate a document or entitle a person to related relief.

predicates.written_transaction_dispute: Parties dispute the effect of a document that purports to record a transaction between them.
predicates.party_alleges_sham_document: A party to the transaction says the document was never intended by the parties to operate.
predicates.party_asserts_different_transaction: That party says the parties made a different transaction from the one recorded in the document.

issues.definition: If a party disputing a written transaction says the document was not intended to operate and that the parties made a different transaction, oral evidence may be admitted to prove that transaction.
